name: Part-List Cueing Effect
description: Giving people some items from a studied list as retrieval cues can make the remaining items harder to recall. Partial help can interfere with a person's own retrieval strategy instead of improving it.
design_relevance_note: Direct digital-design relevance is very limited. At most, it is a caution for hint systems, partial examples, recall-based learning tools, or autocomplete-like supports where supplying some targets may disrupt retrieval of the rest; it is not a mainstream everyday UI principle.
prevalence_note: A classic but highly specialized memory-literature term, almost never named in everyday design practice.

findings.description: A meta-analysis of 109 samples (N=5,605) confirmed the part-list cuing impairment is a robust, medium-sized effect (Cohen's convention), not sensitive to the number of study items, relationship among study items, number of cues provided, or recall time allowed. One genuine moderator found: longer retention periods between study and test actually reduce the impairment -- a real boundary condition on the effect's magnitude, not just a uniform, unconditional impairment.
findings.effect_size: medium (Cohen's d convention; exact pooled value not stated in the abstract)
findings.source_title: Deceitful Hints: a Meta-Analytic Review of the Part-List Cuing Impairment in Recall

findings.description: Review evidence shows that giving a subset of studied items as cues often impairs recall of the remaining items, while also documenting conditions where part-list cuing can facilitate retrieval instead. The effect is real, but not as unconditional as the shorthand sometimes implies.
findings.source_title: The Many Faces of Part-List Cuing—Evidence for the Interplay Between Detrimental and Beneficial Mechanisms
